segment_name: A Woman's Right to Work: Setting the Stakes

questions.question: Daniel, you want to read that 'great reserve' line — 'When one woman vanishes in matrimony, the reserve offers a substitute for the world's work' — as essentially a capitalist recruitment pitch. But isn't there a risk you're being cleverer than Gissing is? Like, is the novel actually indicting Rhoda here, or are you doing the indicting on Gissing's behalf?
questions.intent: Get Rosen to commit hard to his complicity reading and expose its most provocative edge — that Rhoda is unwittingly a tool of capital — so Edmund and Oliver can push back with texture

questions.question: Oliver, you've said these passages are designed to be *spoken* — that Rhoda sounds like she's standing taller as the argument builds. So put that to the test: what does 'It isn't personal feeling that directs a great movement in civilization' actually feel like in her mouth? Because Edmund thinks she's protesting too much, Daniel thinks she's been colonised by economic logic — what do *you* hear when that line lands?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to perform or at least embody the rhetorical force of the line, and use that moment to surface the three-way disagreement about what the line actually *does* to the reader

questions.question: Edmund, you've called Rhoda 'magnificent and slightly tragic' — which is a generous reading. But Daniel's basically saying that generosity is exactly the problem, that we mistake her consistency and conviction for freedom when it's actually just a very elegant trap. How do you answer that without just saying 'yes but she's very compelling'?
questions.intent: Force Leigh to defend his character-study reading against Rosen's structural critique — and draw out his point about Rhoda performing certainty she doesn't fully feel, which is where his and Trevelyan's readings actually overlap

questions.question: Oliver, you flagged that little word 'irritably' in chapter thirteen — Rhoda getting irritable when she has to invoke logic against feeling. Edmund calls it her 'protesting too much.' Daniel would probably say it's the system chafing. But isn't that single adverb doing more work than any of the actual arguments she makes? What does Gissing want us to do with that crack in the armour?
questions.intent: Zoom in on a specific textual moment to ground the abstract disagreement — and surface Trevelyan's point that ideology here functions as emotional armour, which should provoke both other guests

questions.question: Daniel, last one from me on this — Rhoda says 'my work and thought are for the women who do not marry.' Oliver hears weariness there, Edmund hears genuine moral conviction. You'd presumably hear something else. Does Gissing give her any dignity in your reading, or is she just — however smart and however sympathetic — entirely captured?
questions.intent: Push Rosen to either soften or double down on his most challenging claim — that Rhoda has no real exit from the system — and give Edmund and Oliver a clear target to respond to before the segment closes

steering_notes: The three readings here form a genuinely productive triangle: Edmund reads Rhoda psychologically (a woman performing certainty she half-doubts), Daniel reads her structurally (a woman whose liberation is indistinguishable from her exploitation), and Oliver reads her theatrically (a woman whose ideology works because it has to, because vulnerability would destroy her). The segment works best if we resist resolving that triangle — let all three feel partially right and partially insufficient. The 'great reserve' passage and the 'personal feeling' line are the two load-bearing quotes; get them said aloud at least once each. Watch for Edmund and Daniel talking past each other on the question of inner conviction vs. structural position — that's the most generative friction in the room. Keep energy pub-conversational: these are smart people who disagree and enjoy it, not academics scoring points.
cross_engagement_targets: Edmund's claim that Rhoda 'protests too much' — that her certainty is performed — directly maps onto Oliver's theatrical reading but cuts against Daniel's structural one: if she's genuinely uncertain, she's tragic; if she's structurally captured, her uncertainty is beside the point. Get all three to name that difference explicitly.

Daniel's reading of the 'great reserve' metaphor as capitalist logic directly contradicts Edmund's point that Rhoda is 'constructing a personal myth of purpose' — one sees ideology, the other sees psychology. Force them to decide whether those are compatible or mutually exclusive.

Oliver's observation that Rhoda argues from scarcity (the odd women are visible only because married women create a deficit) is a structural point that actually supports Daniel's reading more than Oliver might want to admit — flag this and see if Oliver accepts or resists the alliance.

segment_name: The Comedy of Courtship and Constraint

questions.question: Oliver, you've said these scenes would work brilliantly on stage — that they have the timing and rhythm of live theatre. But you also want to read us that Poppleton passage from chapter eight. So make the case: what is Gissing actually doing there? Is it a joke, or is it something darker wearing a joke's clothes?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to perform the Poppleton passage and articulate the comedy-as-horror thesis — sets up immediate pushback from Daniel about whether calling it 'comedy' lets Widdowson off the hook

questions.question: Daniel, I can hear you bristling a bit at Oliver's framing. Because you've called Widdowson an enforcer — not a buffoon. So when Gissing writes 'by way of mild discipline, he first of all suggested a closer attention to the affairs of the house' — that word 'discipline' — is Gissing exposing a system, or is he writing a portrait of one specific, limited man?
questions.intent: Force the system-vs-individual debate into the open — gets Daniel to read the 'mild discipline' passage and stake out his structural reading, which Edmund will want to contest directly

questions.question: Edmund, you've said the constraint in these scenes flows from human limitation and mutual misunderstanding — not from any social programme. But then there's that line: 'Like most men of his kind, he viewed religion as a precious and powerful instrument for directing the female conscience.' Oliver calls that a scalpel. Does Gissing's 'most men of his kind' let you off the hook? Isn't that precisely a systemic claim?
questions.intent: Use the c15:p53 passage to put pressure on Edmund's psychological reading — the phrase 'most men of his kind' implies a type, not just an individual, and Edmund needs to answer for that

questions.question: Edmund, you made a point I want to push on — you said Everard is himself a caricature, a man who mistakes sexual restlessness for enlightenment. Oliver seems to think the comedy is on Widdowson's side. Daniel thinks the comedy is a kind of alibi for power. But is Everard's mockery of the Poppleton marriage just another form of the same blindness — a man who thinks he's seeing clearly but isn't?
questions.intent: Open up the Everard question and get all three experts reacting — this is where the 'who does Gissing endorse' argument can get heated

questions.question: Oliver, you want to read us Monica's line from chapter seven — 'Yet we have gone against the ordinary rule, and people would make us suffer for it — or me, at all events.' You said that last phrase does all the work. Say more. Because Daniel would say that's the system speaking through Monica, and Edmund would say that's just a woman of unusual clarity seeing her situation plain. Which is it — or does it have to be one thing?
questions.intent: End the segment on Monica's own voice — use c7:p165 to triangulate all three readings and let the experts fight over what Monica's self-awareness actually means

steering_notes: The central tension to cultivate is Oliver's comedy-as-horror thesis versus Daniel's anatomy-of-power reading, with Edmund's psychological individualism as the wild card that irritates both. Don't let this become a debate about whether Gissing is a feminist — keep it grounded in the specific passages and what Gissing's narrator is actually doing in each one. Push back if anyone retreats into abstraction. The best radio comes from getting them to read the lines aloud and then argue about what they just heard. Oliver will want to perform; let him, then turn it over to Daniel fast. Edmund is at his best when he feels the other two are flattening something — give him moments to rescue the individual from the system argument. End on Monica, not on Widdowson.
cross_engagement_targets: Daniel's claim that Widdowson's absurdity is 'the absurdity of power maintaining itself' directly contradicts Oliver's claim that he's a comic grotesque — not a villain or a figure of pathos. Get them to each read the 'women were very like children' line and say what they hear.

Edmund's reading of Monica in c7:p165 ('perfect clarity about the social cost') and Daniel's reading of the same line ('epistemic freedom to know her own mind') are surprisingly close but reach opposite conclusions about what Gissing is indicting — flag this and make them notice they're almost agreeing.

Oliver says the comedy IS the tragedy; Daniel says the comedy is an alibi that masks extraction. These are genuinely incompatible claims about how literary form works, and it's worth slowing down there — not to resolve it, but to make the disagreement audible.

questions.question: Oliver, you called Widdowson a 'comic grotesque' — and I think that's going to raise some eyebrows around this table. Because there's a moment where he's patrolling Mrs. Conisbee's pavement like a beat copper, and yes, it's almost farcical — but you're also saying that's what makes him *unbearable*. Can you read that passage and explain what Gissing is doing with that double register, the comedy sitting right on top of the horror?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to articulate his theatrical grotesque thesis and open the 'is Widdowson tragic or pathological' debate early

questions.question: Edmund, I want to put c19:p37 to you directly — Widdowson's confession, 'I have my faults, I know them only too well.' Oliver's already said that self-awareness without the capacity for change is almost *crueler* than ignorance. You seem to think that passage is the moral heart of the character. Who's right — is that confession evidence of conscience, or is it just the machinery of self-destruction narrating itself?
questions.intent: Force direct confrontation between Leigh's 'moral tragedy' reading and Trevelyan's 'self-awareness is worthless' thesis using the same passage

questions.question: Daniel, Edmund just used the phrase 'the human condition' — and I have a feeling you want to throw something at him when he says that. Because your argument is basically that Gissing is showing us a *system* running its code, not a soul confronting the abyss. Can you take us to c23:p35 — that leap from Virginia's drinking to suspecting Monica — and show us what you mean? Because that's the moment I find most chilling, and I'm not sure it's chilling for the same reasons you do.
questions.intent: Get Rosen to make the structuralist case at its sharpest and provoke Leigh's 'Everyman' counter

questions.question: Oliver, I want you to read c19:p55 — 'every day the distance between them widened' — because all three of you have flagged that passage and you're going to use it to say completely different things. Go ahead and read it, and then tell me: when you hear that rhythm, those short clauses, what is Gissing actually *doing* to the reader there?
questions.intent: Use the shared passage as a pressure point to expose the three divergent readings — theatrical, systemic, moral — in direct competition

questions.question: Edmund, last one, and I'm going to push you here — Daniel says passion is the *alibi*, that 'terrible thoughts' and vigils in the rain aren't tragedy, they're the system working exactly as designed. If you're right that this is about a will corrupted by possessiveness and no social reform fixes that — what does Gissing actually want us to *do* with Widdowson? Pity him? Fear him? Because I'm not sure the novel lets us off the hook with just 'human condition.'
questions.intent: Force Leigh to defend the moral reading against Rosen's systemic critique and resolve whether the novel offers any exit from Widdowson's orbit

steering_notes: The core fault line is Leigh (moral tragedy, individual will) vs Rosen (structural critique, systemic output) with Trevelyan running a third track that holds comedy and horror simultaneously — his theatrical lens is the most mobile and can be deployed to complicate either of the other two. Let Leigh and Rosen go at each other directly on c19:p37 and c23:p35 before pulling Trevelyan back in. The shared passage at c19:p55 is the best single moment for three-way cross-engagement — all three want it, all three hear something different in it. Save c24:p91 as a late-segment gut-punch if energy drops.
cross_engagement_targets: c19:p37: Leigh calls it confession and conscience; Trevelyan calls it self-awareness without transformation — same text, opposite verdicts, direct collision
c19:p55: all three experts have flagged this passage; reading it aloud and then letting each respond in turn will expose the structural vs theatrical vs moral split in one concentrated moment

c23:p35: Trevelyan reads it as theatrical irony (manufacturing the betrayal he fears); Rosen reads it as the system teaching men to suspect all women — push them to argue about whether the pathology is individual or institutional
Rosen's 'passion is the alibi' formulation vs Leigh's 'broken conscience' — these are direct contradictions of the same emotional register in Widdowson and should be named explicitly on air

questions.question: Oliver, you called the physical description of Everard in c8:p18 seductive prose about seduction itself — that the word 'caress' is doing double duty. Can you read that passage and walk us through what you mean? Because I want to understand: is Gissing flattering the reader with beautiful writing, or is he setting a trap?
questions.intent: Get Oliver to read the c8:p18 passage aloud and articulate his 'two registers simultaneously' thesis — the narrator as performer rather than observer

questions.question: Daniel, I want to put something to you directly. Edmund and Oliver both seem to find this narrator admirable — precise, surgical, almost generous. But you're suggesting that the very elegance of c22:p190, the way it dissects Everard so beautifully, is itself a kind of cover. The novel spends all this time in his head. Is Gissing mourning Everard, or is he excusing him?
questions.intent: Force Daniel to name the tension between the narrator's formal sophistication and its ideological effect — draw out the 'accidentally revealing' thesis and provoke Edmund

questions.question: Edmund, you said Everard's failure is constitutional — a failure of will, not a product of his class or his era, and the narrator is clear-eyed about that. But Daniel's just argued the opposite: that self-awareness without consequence is exactly how the system protects men like Everard. Can you read us that line — 'He had not in him the stuff of vigorous rascality' — and tell me why you think Gissing is diagnosing a soul rather than a structure?
questions.intent: Direct confrontation between Edmund's moral-individual reading and Daniel's systemic reading, with the c22:p190 passage as the battlefield

questions.question: Oliver, you want to read the Mary Barfoot passage from c21:p0 — the one about transmuting joys and sorrows into principles. Edmund thinks that's about individual temperament. Daniel thinks Gissing gives us far less of her inner life than he gives Everard. You called the architecture exquisite. So whose Mary is it — the intellectual visionary, the psychological specimen, or the character the novel is quietly sidelining?
questions.intent: Three-way collision on the Mary Barfoot passage — get Oliver to read it, then let Edmund and Daniel fight over what the narrator is actually doing with her

questions.question: Daniel, I want to give you the last word on this before we move on. You've said the narrator's decision to live inside Everard's head tells us something darker than Gissing may have intended. But Oliver would say that's Gissing being generous to the reader — showing us the mechanism. Can those two things both be true? Can a narrator be formally brilliant and ideologically compromised at the same time — or does one cancel the other out?
questions.intent: Push Daniel toward a synthesis or a sharper articulation of his thesis — does formal mastery exonerate or implicate the novel? Good closing provocation for the segment

steering_notes: This segment has a natural three-way tension worth exploiting: Oliver reads the narrator as a virtuoso performer, Edmund reads it as a moralist, Daniel reads it as an ideological apparatus. Don't let them talk past each other — the c22:p190 passage is the shared text they all cite, so use it as a pressure point. Push for readings aloud: Oliver on c8:p18, Edmund or Daniel on c22:p190, Oliver on c21:p0. The pub energy here comes from the fact that all three admire the prose but disagree violently about what it's doing. Keep returning to: 'But what is the narrator actually FOR in this novel?' That question has three genuinely different answers and no easy resolution.
cross_engagement_targets: Oliver says the narrator performs in two registers — seduction then exposure. Daniel says the exposure in c22:p190 is itself a form of seduction: we feel the narrator understands Everard so well that we forgive him. These are directly contradictory readings of the same formal move — push Oliver to respond to Daniel's version explicitly.

Edmund insists Mary's militancy in c13:p122 reveals philosophical precision, not mere polemic. Daniel insists the novel's form then immediately abandons her inner life in favour of Everard's. This is a factual claim about narrative structure as much as interpretation — worth pressing Edmund on whether he disputes Daniel's observation about screen time, or just its significance.

Oliver and Edmund both quote the same line from c22:p190 ('He had not in him the stuff of vigorous rascality') but for opposite purposes: Oliver to show aesthetic irony, Edmund to show moral clarity. Getting them to articulate why they hear the same sentence differently would make excellent radio.

segment_name: Isolation and Atmosphere: The Weight of Choice

questions.question: Oliver, you've said these passages actually *sing* when read aloud — so let's test that. Can you read us the 'Her soul trembled in its nakedness' line from c29:p1, and then tell me what you're hearing in the rhythm that a silent reader would miss?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to perform a close reading aloud and articulate his 'Gissing as entertainer' thesis — opens the door for Daniel to challenge whether beautiful prose aestheticizes suffering

questions.question: Daniel, I want to push you on that word 'semblance' in c29:p46 — you say Gissing knows the difference between freedom and its costume. But Oliver would say the *irony is the point*, that Gissing is being deliberately theatrical about Monica's self-delusion. Isn't there a risk that your reading — where the structures are always the real story — actually flattens what's most interesting about Monica as a character?
questions.intent: Force Rosen to defend his structural reading against the charge that it reduces Monica to a symptom rather than a person — should provoke Trevelyan and Leigh to pile in from opposite directions

questions.question: Edmund, you said Gissing 'grants his characters no political alibis' — which is a strong claim. But Daniel would say that's exactly the ideology at work: making systemic oppression look like personal moral failure. So when we read that Rhoda has 'persuaded herself' in c27:p11 — is that Gissing respecting her moral agency, or is it Gissing letting the system off the hook?
questions.intent: Put Leigh and Rosen into direct collision over whether the novel's refusal of victimhood is a feature or a bug — Trevelyan's voluptuous shame thesis should also surface here

questions.question: Oliver, you made this striking claim that Rhoda is *getting something* from her suffering — that the asceticism in c27:p11 is almost voluptuous. That's a much darker read than 'she's been damaged by patriarchy.' Does Gissing actually like Rhoda's self-destruction a little bit? Is there something uncomfortable in how he writes her cruelty to herself?
questions.intent: Draw out Trevelyan's messiest, most provocative psychological reading — should make both Leigh (who sees moral weakness) and Rosen (who sees structural damage) uncomfortable in different ways

questions.question: Daniel, last one for you — the storms in c25:p0. Oliver hears Gissing showing off, Edmund hears genuine psychological correlative, and you're calling it atmospheric camouflage for class violence. But can all three of those be true at once? Or does something actually get lost if we don't pick a lane?
questions.intent: Force the panel to either synthesize or sharpen their disagreement about the weather imagery — good closing question because it asks all three experts to declare what's actually at stake in how we read atmosphere

steering_notes: The tension between Trevelyan and Rosen is the engine of this segment — Trevelyan thinks beautiful prose doing psychological work is a feature, Rosen thinks it's a politically suspect distraction. Let that run. Leigh is the useful third force: he agrees with Trevelyan that the characters are agents of their own ruin but for moral-spiritual rather than aesthetic reasons, which should annoy both of them. Push the group toward the specific passages rather than general claims — if anyone goes abstract, bring them back to a line. The 'Her soul trembled in its nakedness' phrase is short enough that all three will want to claim it for different purposes; use that.
cross_engagement_targets: Trevelyan's 'voluptuous shame' thesis directly contradicts Rosen's structural damage reading of Rhoda in c27:p11 — both cite the same sentence but read its syntax in opposite directions; get them to argue about who is in control of Rhoda's interiority, Gissing or the system

Leigh and Rosen are on a collision course over moral agency: Leigh says these women choose their ruin, Rosen says that framing is ideological cover. The word 'persuaded herself' in c27:p11 is the exact flashpoint — whose side is Gissing's syntax on?

Trevelyan's claim that the weather in c25:p0 is Gissing showing off as an entertainer sits awkwardly with both Leigh's psychological realism and Rosen's political allegory — all three have incompatible investments in what atmosphere is *for*, and that's worth surfacing explicitly

segment_name: Principle Versus Desire: The Novel's Central Debate

questions.question: Oliver, you said something in our conversation that I keep coming back to — you called this novel 'two kinds of self-deception running in parallel.' Can you take us to that moment in chapter six where Rhoda says women need to revolt against sexual instinct — passage c6:p126 — and tell us what you hear in that line? Because you said Rhoda is absolutely serious and absolutely wrong at the same time. What does that actually sound like on the page?
questions.intent: Get Trevelyan to read and perform c6:p126, establishing his core thesis about prose rhythm as emotional truth — and immediately invite the other two to contest whether 'self-deception' is the right frame

questions.question: Daniel, I suspect you'd want to stop us right there — because you've argued that Rhoda's celibacy isn't really self-deception, it's something more troubling than that. She's not fooling herself; she's been fooled by the whole system. So when Oliver hears wounded pride in that passage, are you hearing something different? What's actually happening when Rhoda says 'revolt against sexual instinct'?
questions.intent: Draw out Rosen's structural critique directly against Trevelyan's psychological reading — create the central disagreement of the segment between individual self-deception and systemic colonization of desire

questions.question: Edmund, you've been patient — and I think you want to blow up both of those readings. You told me before we started that you think your colleagues are going to turn this into a political argument and miss what Gissing is actually doing. You wanted to talk about c22:p1 — 'the independence she had been struggling to assert ever since her marriage meant only freedom to love.' What do you make of that line, and why does it not read to you as evidence of the system trapping Monica?
questions.intent: Give Leigh space to make his moral-tragedy case using the Monica passage — and set up the three-way collision between psychological, structural, and tragic-humanist readings of the same line

questions.question: Daniel, Edmund just said Monica's discovery that freedom means 'freedom to love' is almost Aristotelian — a genuine insight into what freedom actually is. But I remember you describing this exact line as the novel's most devastating exposure of how thoroughly Monica's autonomy has been colonized. Can those two readings both be true at once, or does one of them have to give?
questions.intent: Force the sharpest direct confrontation of the segment — make Rosen and Leigh argue over whether c22:p1 is a moment of authentic self-knowledge or the final proof of ideological capture — Trevelyan can referee with his 'musical tension' thesis

questions.question: Last one — and I want to put this to Oliver first because you said something that's been nagging at me. You said Gissing doesn't resolve the conflict between principle and desire, he shows both sides winning simultaneously. But Daniel's argument is that the whole debate is a false choice — the system has already decided, and both women lose. Edmund thinks it's tragedy in the classical sense — they see clearly and are destroyed anyway. So which is it? Is this novel unresolvable because Gissing is a great artist, or because the situation he's describing has no real exit?
questions.intent: Close the segment by bringing all three theses into collision — Trevelyan's aesthetic irresolution, Leigh's moral tragedy, Rosen's structural determinism — and let the disagreement land without false resolution

steering_notes: The three readings here are genuinely incompatible and that's the gift — Trevelyan reads inward (prose rhythm, self-deception), Leigh reads upward (universal moral psychology), Rosen reads outward (systemic power). Push each of them to speak to the others' framework rather than just reasserting their own. The Monica line from c22:p1 is the pivot passage — all three quoted it in pre-interviews and mean completely different things by it, so use it as the segment's centerpiece. Don't let Leigh and Rosen's disagreement become abstract; keep pulling them back to specific words. Trevelyan is the most likely to generate heat and light at the same time — use him to reframe when the conversation goes too theoretical. Watch for the moment when someone concedes partial ground; that's usually more interesting than the disagreement itself.
cross_engagement_targets: Trevelyan says Rhoda's celibacy is 'wounded pride dressed as principle' — Rosen says it's 'internalized oppression' — these sound similar but have completely different political implications; get them to notice they're almost agreeing and then find where they actually split

Leigh and Rosen both quote c22:p1 as their key Monica passage but read it as opposite things — Leigh as liberation, Rosen as colonization — this needs to be staged as a direct confrontation over the same words

Trevelyan's claim that Gissing is 'amused' by these women and Rosen's warning that sympathy for inner life can 'make oppression beautiful' are in direct tension — push Trevelyan to respond to the political stakes of his aesthetic position

All three agree both women are self-deceived in some sense; the productive question is whether that self-deception is authored by the women themselves, by their circumstances, or by the novel's own sentimental structure — nobody said this explicitly in pre-interviews but it's where the argument is actually heading

segment_name: The Odd Women's Persistence and Paradox

questions.question: Edmund, let's start with the sentence that seems to crack the whole novel open. Monica says — and I want to read this exactly — 'I should never have married him if I hadn't been tempted by the thoughts of living easily—and I feared so—that I might always be alone.' When you hear that, does it feel like a defeat for the feminist argument, or does it feel like the feminist argument finally telling the truth about itself?
questions.intent: Draw out Leigh's core take that Monica's fear exposes something ideology can't fix, and prime Rosen to push back that this 'truth' is actually a systemic trap rather than a human failing

questions.question: Daniel, you want to read that Rhoda line — 'Think bravely and nobly of yourself!' — and then immediately ask what happens when your bravery runs up against an institution that won't pay you. But Oliver would probably say the line is rhetorically alive, genuinely moving, even if it bounces off Monica's despair like rain off stone. So which is it — is Rhoda's voice powerful or is it wishful thinking dressed up as power?
questions.intent: Force direct engagement between Rosen's structural critique and Trevelyan's aesthetic appreciation of Rhoda's rhetoric — get them disagreeing about whether beauty and political inadequacy can coexist in the same sentence

questions.question: Oliver, you said something in our chat that stuck with me — that Gissing is a novelist of performance and failure, that he gives characters magnificent words so we can watch those words fail. But doesn't that reading let Gissing off the hook a little? If it's all dark comedy about rhetoric bouncing off stone walls, are we just aestheticising women's suffering?
questions.intent: Push Trevelyan to defend his aesthetic reading against the charge that it depoliticises the novel — also opens space for Rosen to pile in with the systemic critique

questions.question: Daniel, I want to take you to the Mary Barfoot scene — c13:p118 — where she reads out that anonymous clerk's letter. You say she's not dismissing his anger, she's exposing that the system forces men and women to compete and then blames women for it. But Edmund would say the novel is actually being generous to the clerk's argument, taking it seriously rather than using it as a punching bag. Who's right — is Mary winning that argument or is Gissing making it genuinely harder to call?
questions.intent: Set up Leigh versus Rosen on the question of whether Gissing's narrative fairness is ideologically neutral or itself a political act — get Leigh to defend his 'no propaganda' reading against Rosen's structural reading

questions.question: Right, so let's end here — because I think there's a real disagreement on the table. Rhoda says to Monica, 'We seemed to have lost you; but before long you will be one of us again' — and you've flagged that little hesitation, that 'I mean,' as the moment abstract ideology meets one broken woman. Is that hesitation Gissing doubting Rhoda, or Rhoda doubting herself — and does the novel actually believe Monica can be recovered?
questions.intent: Bring the segment to a point of productive irresolution by pressing Trevelyan on whether the novel endorses recovery or treats it as another beautiful, insufficient gesture — invite Leigh and Rosen to take opposing sides on what Gissing actually believes

steering_notes: The central tension is between Trevelyan's aesthetic-tragic reading (magnificent words failing beautifully), Leigh's humanist reading (ideology can't heal the fearful soul), and Rosen's structural reading (the whole conversation is managed by capitalism). Don't let any one frame dominate too early — the segment gets good radio when all three are in the air simultaneously and the experts are forced to account for each other. Push back on Trevelyan if he aestheticises too cleanly; push back on Rosen if the structural argument becomes too schematic; push back on Leigh if 'tragic realism' starts to sound like political resignation. The Monica confession line is the pivot point — keep returning to it.
cross_engagement_targets: Trevelyan and Rosen are on a collision course over Rhoda's 'Think bravely' speech: Trevelyan finds it theatrically alive and carries its own insufficiency as a kind of tragic beauty; Rosen sees it as ideologically complicit, demanding individual transcendence while the system stays intact. Make them address this directly.

Leigh and Rosen disagree about what Gissing's narrative fairness means politically — Leigh reads it as refusing propaganda, Rosen would say studied neutrality is itself a position that protects the status quo. The Mary Barfoot letter scene is the flashpoint.

Trevelyan and Leigh are closer than they think — both resist partisan readings — but Trevelyan locates the novel's power in performance and gap, while Leigh locates it in moral imagination and the irreducibility of human fear. Get them to notice where they diverge.
